Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology and etiology of inflammatory arthropathy and Lyme arthritis in the
pediatric population.
Perform an appropriate work up of pediatric patients in whom inflammatory arthropathy or
Lyme arthritis is suspected.
Specify the role of the pediatric orthopaedic surgeon in the management of inflammatory
arthropathy and Lyme arthritis.
Differentiate between Lyme arthritis and septic arthritis.


Overview
Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in the United States and Europe.
Lyme disease was first described in 1977 by Steere et al1 in a report of 39 children and
12 adults all located within a small radius in Connecticut. In the original report, Lyme
arthritis was the common finding; however, additional research has shown that Lyme
disease may affect almost all systems of the body.
Lyme disease commonly is associated with erythema migrans, a circular or ovoid lesion
at the site of a tick bite, typically occurring between 1 and 31 days after exposure (mean,
10 days after exposure).2 Other skin manifestations include multiple erythema migrans
rashes, which may represent disseminated disease, and acrodermatitis chronica
atrophicans, which suggests a chronic infection.3 Nervous system involvement may
occur and is called neuroborreliosis. Lyme carditis is less common but may result in
arrhythmias. Lyme arthritis is the most common presenting symptom in patients with
acute Lyme disease, and recognition by the orthopaedic provider is essential to aid in
early detection and management.

Epidemiology
Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne illness in the United States, and its
incidence has continued to increase since it was originally reported in the 1970s, with
the current estimated incidence being 300,000 cases annually.4 Despite the discovery of
Lyme disease in all 50 states, a regional distribution of 10 states (Connecticut, Delaware,
Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island,
and Wisconsin) is responsible for 93% of all cases.5 Recently, the geographic range has
expanded to states neighboring these states with a high incidence.4 Connecticut remains
the area of highest incidence, with reports of 73.6 cases per 100,000 people. Lyme
disease is associated with a bimodal age distribution. The highest annual mean rate is in
children aged 5 to 15 years, and the second peak is in individuals aged 45 to 55 years.
Confirmed cases are slightly more common in males. Infections have been diagnosed at

all times of year; however, most cases present between June and August. Increased time
outdoors is associated with an increased risk of Lyme disease; however, many patients
do not recall a specific tick bite. This is particularly true in pediatric patients, in whom a
thorough history of tick exposure may be more challenging to obtain (Figure 1).


Pathophysiology
Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness with a well-understood pathogenesis. Symptomatic
disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is carried by the Ixodes
tick. Rodents and other small mammals are natural carriers of B burgdorferi and the
preferred host for the Ixodes tick. If the Ixodes tick feeds on a small mammal infected
with B burgdorferi, the tick becomes a carrier of the spirochete and can transmit it to a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lyme Disease and Inflammatory Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001053
3/27

human via a bite.6 Transmission of the spirochete from the tick to the human typically
takes 48 to 72 hours; therefore, transmission is rare if ticks are attached for less than 24
hours.7 After infection, the spirochete multiplies locally within the dermis and then
undergoes hematogenous dissemination to multiple sites, commonly the skin, joints,
and central nervous system.8
During systemic dissemination, B burgdorferi interacts with host cell surfaces by binding
to integrins, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins within cellular and extracellular matrices.
Despite the activation of host immune defenses, the spirochete can evade detection by
modulating surface antigen expression and suppressing immune pathways. After
dissemination, B burgdorferi may remain localized to tissue niches for extended periods
of time, with or without clinical symptoms. In the United States, B burgdorferi is the sole
etiologic agent and contributes to approximately 60% of untreated individuals in whom
episodic large-joint arthritis, particularly in the knees, develops within months of initial
infection.4,9
Lyme arthritis typically occurs months after infection. Spirochetes disseminate and
invade the synovium of large joints, at which locations they trigger a local inflammatory
reaction10 Synovial hypertrophy, vascular proliferation, and increased cellular density
result in localized joint pain and effusion. The mechanism of joint damage is not as
clearly elucidated.
Classification
Although no true classification system for Lyme disease exists, the disease is divided into
distinct clinical stages consisting of early localized, early disseminated, and late Lyme disease.
Early Localized Lyme Disease

Early Localized Lyme Disease
Early localized disease is typified by erythema migrans. The rash commonly occurs 1 to
31 days after infection with B burgdorferi. After initial appearance as a small red macule,

9/3/26, 4:36 PM
AAOS | Lyme Disease and Inflammatory Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001053
4/27

the rash expands over the course of several days before central clearing occurs, giving
rise to the classic bull’s-eye appearance. Early localized disease may be accompanied by
general malaise, fatigue, and headache. Within the pediatric population, the rash is most
frequently observed on the head and neck (26%), the extremities (25%), and the back
(24%). The rash less frequently occurs on the abdomen (9%), axilla (8%), groin (5%), or
chest (3%).11
Early Disseminated Lyme Disease

Early Disseminated Lyme Disease
Early disseminated disease occurs days to months after an initial tick bite and is more
commonly associated with nervous system and cardiac involvement.12 Most patients
with early disseminated disease do not have a history of erythema migrans, and
neurologic or cardiac findings frequently are the initial presenting symptom. Typically,
secondary erythema migrans lesions present as pale, uniform lesions on the face and
extremities. Observed in 17% to 57% of patients, this distribution indicates the
hematogenous/lymphatic dissemination of B burgdorferi.9,13
Late Lyme Disease

Late Lyme Disease
Late Lyme disease presents with more diffuse involvement of multiple systems. Arthritis
is the most identifying feature of late Lyme disease, typically occurring months after
disease onset.14 In addition to articular involvement, late Lyme disease frequently
results in dermatologic, cardiac, and neurologic manifestations. Lyme arthritis is the
most common finding of late-stage Lyme disease in the pediatric population. Children
are more prone to Lyme arthritis after infection by B burgdorferi compared with adults.
In a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance study conducted between
2008 and 2015, Lyme arthritis was observed in 27.5% of patients and was most common

in patients aged 10 to 14 years.4 In a small number of patients, chronic inflammatory
arthritis resembling rheumatoid arthritis may emerge, referred to as postinfectious
Lyme arthritis.15
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination

Patient History and Physical Examination
The orthopaedic surgeon typically is involved in the diagnosis of Lyme disease if it
presents as Lyme arthritis. This is of particular importance because Lyme arthritis may
closely resemble acute bacterial septic arthritis; however, the management of the two
disorders are very disparate. Both disorders most commonly are associated with a
single, large joint effusion with associated pain and limitations in range of motion. Only
one-third of patients who present with a rash recall a tick bite within the preceding
month, and most children with Lyme arthritis do not recall an antecedent rash.11 Given
that a tick bite rarely is determined during the patient history, the evaluating provider
should focus questions on outdoor activity and potential exposure rather than a specific
history of a tick bite.
In distinguishing Lyme arthritis from bacterial septic arthritis, several key differences are
important to determine. Children may present with fever and limited–weight bearing.
Septic arthritis is most commonly observed in the hip, whereas Lyme arthritis is much
more commonly observed in the knee (up to 90%); however, both disorders may occur in
almost any joint.16,17 Patients with Lyme arthritis are more likely to present afebrile and
are less likely to refuse to bear weight.18 Abnormal synovium and more joint effusion is
observed on the MRIs of patients with Lyme arthritis, whereas soft-tissue edema and
osseous changes are observed on the MRIs of patients with septic arthtitis.18 Joint
arthrocentesis should be performed but does not always distinguish between the two
diseases.

Laboratory Evaluation

Laboratory Evaluation
Lyme serology is the preferred method for diagnosis; however, several days are required
to obtain a result, which makes it less useful in differentiating Lyme arthritis from
bacterial septic arthritis. This delay is associated with a risk of unnecessary surgical
management because Lyme arthritis, which generally is managed via oral antibiotic
agents, may be mistaken for septic arthritis, which requires immediate surgical
management and débridement to reduce the risk of irreversible joint destruction. The
rate of surgical treatment in patients with positive Lyme serologic tests and a negative
bacterial infection ranges from 10% to 32%19,20 and these events are associated with
increased hospital length of stay and increased cost of hospital admission. These
findings underscore the importance of rapid diagnostic tools for Lyme arthritis, such as
enzyme immunoassays. In a cohort of 10 patients with acute septic arthritis, three
patients had positive enzyme immunoassay results within 1 hour, leading to cancellation
of planned surgical irrigation and débridement. Instead, these patients were placed
under observation for 48 hours in combination with the administration of intravenous
ceftriaxone for the management of Lyme arthritis.21
A US FDA report released in July 2019 approved the use of new serologic assays under a
modified two-tiered testing strategy. This method involves the use of two sequential
enzyme immunoassays to detect antigens in vivo.22 Clinically, modified two-tiered
testing compared with the standard two-tier protocol is associated with a higher rate of
positive test results in adults.23 Although these enzyme immunoassays hold promise in
streamlining Lyme arthritis diagnosis by improving test specificity, they offer limited
advances with regard to sensitivity, particularly in the initial stages of the disease. A
recent retrospective study reported that rapid fluorescent immunoassay is in high
concordance with the two-tier testing strategy and helps quickly distinguish Lyme
disease from similar musculoskeletal conditions, leading to earlier diagnosis and
avoidance of unnecessary surgical treatment, hospital admission, and antibiotic
agents.24

7/27

Laboratory tests that measure inflammation, including white blood cell (WBC) count, C-
reactive protein (CRP) level, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), should be
obtained. Patients with Lyme disease have a lower mean WBC count, CRP level, and ESR
compared with patients who have bacterial septic arthritis; however, both groups have
mean levels above the upper limit of normal. Thompson et al18 reported that children
with Lyme arthritis had a mean WBC count of 10.9 × 103 μL, a mean CRP level of 3.6
mg/dL, and a mean ESR of 44.6 mm/hr, whereas children with septic arthritis had a
mean WBC count of 12.4 × 103 μL, a mean CRP level of 11.4 mg/dL, and a mean ESR of
62.7 mm/hr. Similarly, Milewski et al16 found lower mean WBCs count in patients with
Lyme arthritis compared with patients with septic arthritis; however no statistically
significant difference in CRP level or ESR was reported between the two groups.
Aspirate results also differed between Lyme arthritis and septic arthritis; however, both
remained elevated. In Lyme arthritis, the mean nucleated cell count was 60,200
cells/mm3 with a differential 61%, whereas in septic arthritis, the mean nucleated cell
count was 123,000 cells/mm3 with a differential of 65%.16 Four clinical criteria may be
used to assess the likelihood of septic arthritis in the knee in the pediatric patient
population: (1) joint pain with a restricted arc of motion, (2) a reported history of a fever,
(3) a CRP level greater than 4 mg/L, and (4) patient age younger than 2 years.25 In this
model, Baldwin et al25 highlighted that the probability of septic arthritis increases
progressively with the number of criteria met¬: zero with no criteria satisfied, 18% with
one criterion satisfied, 45% with two criteria satisfied, 84% with three criteria satisfied,
and 100% with all four criteria satisfied. In patients who do not fit these criteria, the
authors recommend Lyme serologic tests.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Traditionally, imaging studies have not been used for the diagnosis of Lyme
arthritis; however, more recent studies have elucidated key differences using
MRI.26 Plain radiography, ultrasonography, and CT may be used to rule out
other etiologies of joint effusion; however, these modalities are not associated
with diagnostic power.

8/27

Ecklund et al26 reviewed MRIs of the knee and identified three considerably
different variables between Lyme arthritis and bacterial septic arthritis. Patients
with Lyme arthritis had notable absence of subcutaneous edema and notable
presence of myositis and popliteal lymphadenopathy. Each finding was an
independent predictor of Lyme arthritis, with the most dependable finding
being the absence of subcutaneous edema. Recent imaging studies conducted
by Yen et al27 suggested that these MRI findings in combination with clinical
indicators, specifically the ability to bear weight and a CRP level less than 3
mg/L, substantially improved the rate of Lyme arthritis detection. Multivariate
analysis demonstrated a progressive increase in the probability of Lyme arthritis
based on the number of criteria present: 35% with one criterion satisfied, 92%
with three criteria satisfied, and 100% with five criteria satisfied.27
Management
Medical Management

Medical Management
In general, Lyme arthritis is successfully managed via medical management, specifically
oral antibiotic agents. The first line of treatment for children is 50 mg/kg of amoxicillin
per day divided into three doses (maximum, 500 mg per dose) or 30 mg/kg of
cefuroxime axetil per day divided into two doses (maximum, 500 mg per dose). In
addition, 4 mg/kg of doxycycline per day divided into two doses (maximum, 100 mg per
dose) is recommended.28 Currently, the American Academy of Pediatrics allows for the
use of 21 days of doxycycline in children younger than 8 years because adequate
evidence does not show that it causes gum hypoplasia and tooth discoloration, which is
the main concern in patients in this age group.22 A single course of oral antibiotic agents
typically is sufficient to resolve symptoms. In the rare instance that oral antibiotic agents
cannot be used, 50 to 75 mg/kg of intravenous ceftriaxone per day as a single dose

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001053
9/27

(maximum, 2 g daily) is the preferred regimen. Cefotaxime and penicillin G may serve as
alternative therapy.
Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon

Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon
The orthopaedic surgeon’s role is the diagnosis of Lyme arthritis, particular in
distinguishing Lyme arthritis from bacterial septic arthritis. A thorough patient history
and physical examination in combination with laboratory workup and, frequently, joint
aspiration are essential for the diagnostic evaluation of Lyme arthritis. MRI may be useful
if the knee is involved, assessing for the classic periarticular lymphadenopathy pattern.27
Nonsurgical Management
The management of Lyme arthritis, similar to Lyme disease, is almost universally medical
management, specifically with oral antibiotic agents.
Surgical Management

Surgical Management
Minimal evidence supports surgical treatment in the management of Lyme disease. The
only reported surgical procedure is synovectomy in patients with chronic, antibiotic
refractory Lyme arthritis. Such patients may have more of an inflammatory response
than an infectious etiology. Younger patients (mean age 5.3 years) with an elevated
synovial WBC count (76.3 × 103/μL) and patients admitted for orthopaedic surgery are
more likely to undergo surgical treatment, with a rate of 74%.19 Synovectomy may be
considered if antibiotic agents are ineffective and as second-line management after anti-
inflammatory medication. For antibiotic resistant Lyme arthritis, disease-modifying
antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and intraarticular corticosteroids have been shown to

afford symptom relief and clinical resolution.29,30 Shoen et al29 reported on 20 patients
who underwent synovectomy for refractory Lyme arthritis and found that joint
inflammation resolved within 1 month of surgical treatment in 80% of the patients.
Surgical management is reserved for patients in whom medical management fails and
rarely is required. Delayed diagnosis of Lyme arthritis and misdiagnosis of Lyme arthritis
as septic arthritis have led to unnecessary surgical management, which underscores the
need for better rapid diagnostic tests.20
Inflammatory Arthritis

Overview
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a broad term applied to a group of conditions
consisting of inflammation of unknown etiology lasting longer than 6 weeks in patients
younger than 16 years.31 Before the term JIA was adopted, various diagnostic terms
were used, with significant overlap. The International League of Associations for
Rheumatology defined JIA and classified the disorder into seven mutually exclusive
subtypes. Collectively, the subtypes share the common findings of inflammation-
mediated joint destruction but otherwise vary widely with regard to phenotypic
presentation. All forms of JIA can negatively affect health-related quality of life and pose
a risk of irreversible joint damage.32 JIA may persist into adulthood, contributing to
sustained morbidity and impairments in functional status and psychosocial well-being.
Less favorable long-term outcomes are observed in patients with early hip or wrist
involvement, symmetric disease, positive rheumatoid factor, or prolonged systemic
inflammation.32

Epidemiology
Reports on the incidence of JIA vary widely, largely because of the variable incidence in
populations studied. Most reports reflect populations of predominantly white cohorts in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:36 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001053
11/27

North America and Europe, with an incidence rate ranging from 1.9 to 23 cases per
100,000 people.33 Oligoarthritis is the most common subtype, accounting for
approximately 30% of JIA cases, with a reported incidence of 3.7 cases per 100,000
people. Less commonly observed subtypes include polyarthritis (1.6 cases per 100,000
people); systemic arthritis (0.6 cases per 100,000 people); and psoriatic arthritis (0.5
cases per 100,000 people).34 The overall incidence of JIA is much higher in females than
in males, nearing a 2:1 ratio;34 the notable exception is the enthesitis-related arthritis
subtype, which is more common in males.35

Pathophysiology
The specific mechanism of JIA remains a focus of research; however, within the past
decade, substantial discoveries have been made, including confirmation that the
systemic subtype of JIA is distinct from the other subtypes with respect to pathogenesis.
Similar to most autoimmune disorders, the cause of JIA is presumed to be multifactorial,
including genetic predisposition and environmental triggers. Concordance rates in
monozygotic twins ranging from 20% to 40% suggest a high genetic component.36
Responsible genes have been identified from HLA-related and non–HLA-related genes.
HLA-related genes associated with JIA include HLA-A2, HLA-B27, HLA-DRB1 and HLA-
DP.37 Non–HLA-related genes associated with JIA include PTPN22, MIF, SLC11A6, WISP3,
and tumor necrosis factor-alpha.38 Multiple environmental triggers have been proposed;
however, no conclusive studies have confirmed specific triggers of the autoreactive
response.
Systemic JIA has a distinct imbalance between proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory
cytokines, suggesting that systemic JIA is more of an autoinflammatory disease than an
autoimmune disease. Systemic JIA is associated with elevated levels of key interleukins
(IL), specifically IL-1, IL-2, and IL-6. Classic findings of autoimmune disorders, including
autoantibodies and autoreactive T-lymphocytes, are not noted in patients with systemic
JIA. The primary cells involved are macrophages and neutrophils, suggesting that

systemic JIA has key differences from the remaining subtypes and successful medical
management may require different medications.39

Histopathology
JIA is characterized by chronic joint inflammation and tissue destruction. Within affected
joints, the synovial membrane thickens because of synoviocyte hyperplasia and
hypertrophy in combination with infiltration by immune cells, including T-cells, B-cells,
neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, and plasma cells.40 This inflammatory activity
leads to intra-articular hypoxia and triggers abnormal angiogenesis, which is marked by
elevated levels of vascular endothelial growth factor, its soluble vascular endothelial
growth factor receptors, osteopontin, and angiopoietin-1.41 The resulting
neovascularization enhances blood flow to the synovium, promoting the additional influx
of pro-inflammatory cells into the joint space. Cytokine activity drives the production of
matrix-degrading enzymes in articular cartilage, leading to loss of function.42 Similarly,
the activation of receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B–expressing osteoclasts
contributes to bone erosion.43 These mechanisms progressively damage cartilage and
bone, resulting in limited joint mobility and impaired skeletal growth.
Classification

Classification
The International League of Associations for Rheumatology classified JIA into seven
subtypes31: systemic arthritis, oligoarthritis, RF-negative polyarthritis, RF-positive
polyarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, enthesitis-related arthritis, and undifferentiated arthritis.
This classification system includes variables, such as the number of affected joints, the
presence of symptoms (eg, fever or rash), and the identification of inflammatory
markers, to differentiate between JIA subtypes.41

Systemic Arthritis

Systemic Arthritis
Systemic arthritis is characterized by arthritis of one or more joints with associated daily
fever for a minimum of 2 weeks. Diagnosis also requires at least one of the following:
evanescent erythematous rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly or
splenomegaly, and serositis. Serositis is most frequently pericarditis with pericardial
effusion; however, it also may manifest as pleuritis or peritonitis. The most commonly
involved joints include the knee (68%), wrist (68%), and ankle (57%).44 Systemic arthritis
is distinct from the other subtypes in that it is an autoinflammatory arthritis, lacking the
typical findings of autoantibodies. Males and females are equally affected.
Oligoarthritis

Oligoarthritis
Oligoarthritis affects one to four joints at onset (within the first 6 months). The persistent
type of oligoarthritis continues to affect only one to four joints; the extended type of
oligoarthritis may grow to include more than four joints over time. Oligoarthritis is the
most common type of JIA and frequently involves the knee, with ankle, subtalar joint,
and elbow involvement in decreasing incidence.45 Inflammation of the eye (uveitis) also
may occur in patients with oligoarticular JIA.41 Small joints of the hands or feet, hips, and
cervical spine typically are spared. The more common age of onset is 2 to 4 years, with
diagnosis after 6 years being rare. Females are affected more often than males by a ratio
of 3:1,41 with an incidence ratio of 4:1.
RF-Negative Polyarthritis

RF-Negative Polyarthritis

RF-negative polyarthritis affects five or more joints and is associated with the finding of a
negative rheumatoid factor test. Large and small joints, the temporomandibular joint,
and the cervical spine are commonly involved. RF-negative disease is diagnosed at a
younger age compared with RF-positive disease, with a biphasic peak of onset. The first
peak is similar to that of oligoarticular JIA, occurring at age 1 to 4 years, and the second
peak occurs at age 6 to 12 years.46
RF-Positive Polyarthritis

RF-Positive Polyarthritis
RF-positive polyarthritis is similar to its RF-negative counterpart in that it affects large
and small joints, the temporomandibular joint, and cervical spine. RF-positive
polyarthritis more closely resembles the adult diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, and the
age of onset typically is older than 8 years. Hip involvement is a poor prognostic factor.
Psoriatic Arthritis

Psoriatic Arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis most commonly is an asymmetric oligoarthritis and may include large
and small joints. Psoriatic skin rash is present in only 13% to 43% of patients at the time
of diagnosis but may occur later in the disease process. Given the relatively low
frequency of classic skin findings, other diagnostic criteria, including a family history of
psoriasis (69%), nail pitting (67%), and dactylitis (39%), are more common.47 Nail
involvement associated with psoriatic arthritis has been linked to distal interphalangeal
joint degeneration and suggests a shared inflammatory mechanism. In a cohort of 69
patients, Williamson et al48 observed that patients with severe nail disease were more
likely to exhibit extensive skin involvement, accelerated joint degeneration, and greater
functional impairment.

Enthesitis-Related Arthritis

Enthesitis-Related Arthritis
Enthesitis-related arthritis is unique in that it is more frequently observed in males than
females. Diagnostic criteria include arthritis/enthesitis with two or more of the following:
sacroiliac tenderness, human leukocyte antigen B27 positivity (observed in 50% of
patients), anterior uveitis, and a family history of ankylosing spondylitis.31 Common
locations of enthesitis include the tibial tubercle, iliac crest, patella (superior or inferior
pole), and the heel (at the Achilles tendon insertion or the origin of the plantar fascia).
The peak age of onset is between 10 to 12 years.
Undifferentiated Arthritis
The classification of undifferentiated arthritis is reserved for any JIA that does not fit into the
diagnostic criteria of the aforementioned subtypes or that meets the criteria for two or more
of the aforementioned subtypes. (Table 1)

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination

Patient History and Physical Examination
JIA is best managed by a pediatric rheumatologist; however, initial presenting complaints
of joint pain frequently result in primary assessment by an orthopaedic surgeon. A
thorough patient history must be obtained, with particular focus on the joints involved,
the duration of symptoms, and the timing of maximal involvement. The most common
symptom is joint stiffness that worsens with inactivity. Stiffness is most pronounced in
the morning. Parents of young children may notice an abnormal gait in the morning that
improves over the course of the day or limited range of joint motion during diaper
changes. Focal joint swelling and specific joint pain often are present but less reliably
noted by families and young children. Findings from the physical examination that are
suggestive of active arthritis include joint effusion, warmth, limited range of motion,
tenderness, and surrounding erythema.49 Other common orthopaedic etiologies of joint
pain, such as trauma; septic arthritis; slipped femoral capital epiphysis; and localized
tendinopathies, including Osgood-Schlatter disease, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease,
and Sever disease, should be ruled out. JIA has common extra-articular manifestations
that may aid in differentiating it from localized musculoskeletal complaints. The most
common extra-articular finding is uveitis, which is observed in approximately 20% of
patients of JIA, with the highest prevalence in patients with oligoarticular arthritis.50

Patients with systemic JIA also may have pericarditis, pleuritis, peritonitis, hepatitis, and
anemia.
Laboratory Evaluation

Laboratory Evaluation
Routine laboratory studies are commonly normal in patients with JIA, which may
complicate the diagnostic process. Even the classic inflammatory laboratory tests, such
as WBC, CRP level, and ESR, commonly are within normal limits or only minimally
elevated, especially in patients with oligoarthritis. More specific rheumatologic
laboratory tests should be ordered by a rheumatologist after clinical evaluation. These
serologic studies include antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated
peptide, and human leukocyte antigen B27 tests. A positive rheumatoid factor or anti-
cyclic citrullinated peptide test correlate with poorer prognosis.51,52
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
JIA is a clinical diagnosis; however, routine imaging studies may aid in excluding other
causes of joint pain in pediatric patients, such as osteomyelitis. Plain radiographs
frequently are normal; however, soft-tissue swelling may be noted. The classic
radiographic findings of periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, and bony
erosions typically are only detected in patients with long-standing disease and are
indicators of poor prognosis.53
Advanced imaging studies, such as MRI, are useful in delineating the extent of synovitis;
however, no specific diagnostic criteria exist. Navallas et al54 highlighted current efforts
to develop and validate these tools, with an MRI scoring system for the
temporomandibular joint serving as a model for broader application in pediatric

rheumatology. The role of CT is limited in JIA. Ultrasonography also may be used to
delineate the extent of synovitis or to assess for effusion in patients with active arthritis;
however, this imaging modality has a minimal role in diagnosis.
Management

Management
The treatment goals in patients with JIA are to minimize joint inflammation and maximize
patient activity. Management may be complex and is best organized by a pediatric
rheumatologist working with a team consisting of ophthalmology, physical therapy,
occupational therapy, nutrition, psychology, and orthopaedic surgery.
Medical Management

Medical Management
Medical management is the mainstay of the management of JIA and typically is
orchestrated by the pediatric rheumatologist. If an orthopaedic surgeon has a high
clinical suspicion of JIA and the patient is awaiting rheumatologic evaluation, NSAIDs and
physical therapy may be initiated before diagnosis.
Nonpharmacologic treatment options include activity modifications and physical and
occupational therapy. Most JIA symptoms improve with activity; therefore, mobility is
emphasized. Acutely symptomatic joints may require rest or limited–weight bearing;
however, activity should be resumed as tolerated. Physical therapy and occupational
therapy are useful in improving and maintaining joint range of motion. Low-impact or
aquatic therapy modalities are useful in patients with considerable pain-limited
activity.45

Commonly used medication classes include corticosteroids, DMARDs, NSAIDs, and
biologics. Biologic medications are those that use a portion of the body’s natural
immune system to manage a disease. For JIA, biologic medications include T-cell
inhibitors, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, IL-1 antagonists, and IL-6 antagonists.
In 2011, the American College of Rheumatology published recommendations on the
pharmacologic strategy for the management of JIA.53 Most children are initially
prescribed NSAIDs, and intra-articular corticosteroids may be used for acute joint
inflammation. In children with persistently high disease activity, the next stage includes
initiation of a DMARD, most frequently methotrexate. Additional DMARDs, including
sulfasalazine and leflunomide, may be prescribed if methotrexate is not tolerated or
ineffective. A biologic agent may be added if patients have an inadequate clinical
response to the initiation of nonbiologic DMARDs. First-line biologics for the
management of JIA are tumor necrosis factor inhibitors; however, other biologics may be
prescribed in patients with a poor clinical response. An important consideration with
regard to the long-term prescription of biologic agents is the risk for opportunistic
infections and malignancy in response to immune suppression.40
Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon

Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon
The most common orthopaedic manifestations of JIA include synovitis, growth
abnormalities, cervical spine arthritis or instability, and joint destruction. Growth
abnormalities may vary widely in patients with JIA. Longitudinal deformities may occur
for various reasons. Localized inflammation adjacent to the physis may result in
premature closure. The most common deformity is affected limb overgrowth from the
distal femoral and proximal tibial physes secondary to chronic knee inflammation and
increased blood flow. Angular deformities may result from asymmetric physeal arrest or
asymmetric overgrowth.

Nonsurgical Management

Nonsurgical Management
The orthopaedic surgeon frequently is the first line of evaluation, particularly in patients
with oligoarthritis. A thorough patient history and physical examination and timely
referral to a pediatric rheumatologist are helpful in efficient diagnosis of JIA. Most
pediatric rheumatologists determine whether nonsurgical management of JIA is
appropriate; however, physical therapy and NSAIDs may be recommended if a high
clinical suspicion for JIA exists and rheumatologic evaluation is pending. A randomized
clinical trial showed that foot orthoses reduce pain and tenderness in patients with foot
and ankle–associated JIA.55
Surgical Management

Surgical Management
Currently, synovectomy is less frequently performed, partly because of the increased
efficacy of medical management and because long-term joint outcome is not affected by
synovectomy.56 Synovectomy mostly is performed in children with active, proliferative
synovitis affecting a small number of joints. Synovectomy may be performed in patients
with focal, large joint refractory synovitis; however, the procedure largely is a
symptomatic surgical procedure without the advantage of preventing joint destruction,
with a reported recurrence rate of 67% to 100%.57
Growth modulation may be required for longitudinal or angular growth deformities
associated with JIA. Hemiepiphysiodesis is the preferred treatment option for angular
deformity; however, if insufficient growth is remaining, then corrective osteotomy may
be performed, with particular care for the increased risk of osteopenia. Timing of
epiphysiodesis for the management of longitudinal deficiency may be complicated by a
systemic disorder because children with JIA may not follow the standard growth
pattern.58

Total joint arthroplasty may be considered in pediatric patients; however, it is less
commonly performed in the pediatric population compared with the young adult
population. Indications for adolescent total joint arthroplasty include severe pain, joint
destruction, and functional limitation after failed medical management. Total hip
arthroplasty is the most commonly performed procedure in the JIA population; however,
total knee arthroplasty, total elbow arthroplasty, and glenohumeral hemiarthroplasty
have been reported.59-61
